title: Black-box unitary synthesis
formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.
status_note: The source question is retained in Rosenthal’s May 2026 revision and the July 2026 Dong–Lombardi–Ma paper. Checked on 2026-09-14. Their bounds concern exponential-time upper bounds or restricted-query lower bounds, not a resolution of the displayed general polynomial-time, constant-diamond-error formulation.

progress.text: Aaronson lists general black-box unitary synthesis as open and distinguishes it from the easier state-preparation task.
Lombardi, Ma and Wright prove a one-query lower bound for general unitary synthesis, with related cryptographic consequences.
Rosenthal’s revised author manuscript presents the exponential-time oracle upper bound and explicitly retains polynomial-time synthesis as Question 1.1.
Dong, Lombardi and Ma give additional one-query separations and approximation results for structured unitaries; the general polynomial-query question remains outside their claimed resolution.

importance.reason: A basic quantum transformation problem under black-box access, clarifying what an oracle interface permits.

sentences: The problem asks whether every quantum unitary can be implemented efficiently using an appropriately chosen Boolean oracle.
One fixed circuit family must work for all unitaries, with the desired unitary encoded only in the oracle.
The implementation must work on arbitrary inputs, including states entangled with an untouched reference.
Both total computation and coherent oracle access must remain polynomial in the number of input qubits.
Known exponential-time implementations and restricted-query lower bounds leave the general question unresolved.

definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.
